replying_to: Replying to BURT: BERT-inspired Universal Representation from Learning Meaningful Segment

content.title: Initial Review
content.review:
[General Review]  
In this paper, the authors propose to improve the BERT by utilizing different levels of linguistic units, which is similar to SpanBERT or BERT with N-gram masking. They propose an N-gram pruning strategy based on PMI calculation to ensure the extracted N-grams are informative. Then a traditional N-gram masking is applied with several minor modifications (some of them are known), such as dynamic masking, etc. The pre-training was performed based on the BERT or BERT-wwm-ext checkpoints with the processed Chinese Wikipedia data. The experiments are carried out on 1) a subset of CLUE, including 6 classification tasks; 2) retrieval-based FAQ; 3) natural language generation. The results show that the proposed BURT model shows marginal improvements over BERT and BERT-wwm-ext.

Overall, the writing of the paper is clear and easy to follow. However, I have several main concerns about this paper, which stop me from recommending acceptance (also see weaknesses in next). 
1) The main results on CLUE is not significant, considering the baselines are not also further pre-trained.
2) The n-gram masking is not a new idea, though the authors try to improve it in some ways.

Also, considering ICLR is one of the top-tier conferences, after evaluating the novelty and impact of the paper, I regrettably decided to recommend to reject this paper.


[Strengths]
1. The authors propose an n-gram refinement strategy for extracting many meaningful n-grams.
2. The writing of the paper is clear and easy to follow.

[Weaknesses]
1. There is a major weakness in the experimental setting, which I think is fatal. The proposed BURT is trained based on the BERT or BERT-wwm-ext checkpoints, but these counterparts were NOT also trained with additional steps for a fair comparison.
2. Besides the major flaws in the experimental setting, the overall gains in the subset of CLUE is limited. Considering the experiments are only performed on a base-level pre-trained language model, I wouldn't call the results are significant.
3. N-gram masking strategy is not a novel idea though the authors try to improve it some way, which I think the novelty is marginal.


[Questions for Authors]
1. Why the evaluations are only performed on a subset of CLUE? I assume that the reading comprehension task (such as CMRC 2018, DRCD) will benefit more from n-gram masking, but there is no result for that. The authors should clarify this.
2. How was the PMI threshold chosen? In Section 2.3.2, it only shows the threshold is -12 but does not describe how it was set.
3. The experiment of SOP in section 3.4 seems weird to me. It is not related to the central idea of this work.


[Minor Comments]
1. page 1: it is better to include citations right after the model names. For e.g., "ELMo, GPT,... (Peters et al., 2018; Radford et al., 2018;...)" -> "ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), GPT (Radford et al., 2018),..."


[Missing Reference]
1. Adam: [Kingma and Ba, 2014] Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. In arXiv.
2. SRILM: [Stolcke, 2002] SRILM - An extensible language modeling toolkit. In ICSLP 2002.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer3
content.comment:
Thanks for the valuable feedbacks.

1.Why the evaluations are only performed on a subset of CLUE?

We are currently running the MRC tasks (CHID, CMRC2018 and C3).  However, it takes nearly 24 hours to fine-tune a single model on a single task such as CHID. At the current pace, we expect that all experimental results will be completed around the ddl of the rebuttal phase.

2.Unfair comparison.

Please refer to Response to Reviewer2.

3.The overall gains in the subset of CLUE is limited.

The focus of this work is to introduce a method that can improve Representation-based Information Retrieval (RIR) tasks. Although CLUE includes tasks that contain sequences of different length, it is not sufficient to reflect the quality and effectiveness of embeddings generated by each model in true situations. Thus, we concentrate more on the retrieval-based FAQ and NLG tasks, which can be accurately done by only manipulating vectors representing the sentences, such as calculating and ranking vector distance in terms of cosine similarity. Overall, our BURT achieves significant improvement on both FAQ and NLG.

3.How was the PMI threshold chosen?

It was updated in Section 3.3.2 Training Details: “After calculating the PMI scores of all n-grams, we try different thresholds from -15 to -10 at 0.5 intervals and evaluate the n-gram vocabulary. We find that when the threshold is high (>=-11.5), nearly 50\% of the n-grams contain 3 ~ 5 characters, and only less than 0.5\% n-grams are longer than 7. Although a lower threshold (<=-12.5) can generate longer n-grams, it will cause too many meaningless n-grams. Therefore, we empirically set the threshold to -12, resulting in 58M n-grams with an average length of 6.4.”

replying_to: Replying to BURT: BERT-inspired Universal Representation from Learning Meaningful Segment
display_title: Experimental results are basically convincing, but the novelty is not sufficiently strong

content.title: Experimental results are basically convincing, but the novelty is not sufficiently strong
content.review:
The authors proposed BURT to capture features of different levels of linguistic unit by extracting and masking n-gram segmentations. In particular, they first (a) extract a large number of n-gram spans from the large corpus and use PMI to filter out meaningless n-gram spans, and second (b) apply masking strategy on those matched n-gram spans and employ the Transformer encoder to predict the tokens in the masked n-gram spans. However, (a) is just a unsupervised method for word segmentation, (b) has been developed in spanBERT, BERT-wwm, ERNIE 2.0, etc. Besides, it is not appropriate to call BURT "universal representation". It did not learn unique embedding for each granularity of linguistic units, nor did it simultaneously learn multiple levels of linguistic units in a single sentence.

    The pros & cons are as follows:

    Pros:

    1. The overall presentation of this paper is clear and the reported experimental results are convincing. The concrete examples and illustrations are also good to tell the methods and experiments.
    2. With the provided implementation details including the used third-party libraries for pre-processing the data and the hyper-parameters for training the model, the reproducibility of this work should not be a problem.
    3. The improvements of BURT compared with its baselines on WSC and the FAQ are significant and convincing.

    Cons:

    1.  As aforementioned, the contribution and novelty of this paper do not seem to be sufficient to be accepted as a ICLR paper.
    2. The "universal representation" is somewhat overclaimed.
    3. According to the experimental results on the test set of CLUE, the improvement of BURT is not that significant except for WSC. Besides, can you explain why BURT achieves great improvement on WSC but not on other tasks in CLUE?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to Reviewer4
content.comment:
Thanks for the valuable feedbacks.

1.The "universal representation" is somewhat overclaimed.

The focus of this work is to introduce the Representation-based Information Retrieval (RIR) task. To this end, we introduce our method and refer to it as “universal representation” because the model is able to first embed different sized sequences into the same vector space, and then retrieve the correct answer given a query from a set of candidates according to vector distance (i.e., cosine similarity). We will consider changing the name if we can come up with a more suitable one. Nevertheless, we have already shown its great significance in two real-life applications.

2.Why BURT achieves great improvement on WSC compared with tasks?

WSC is a coreference resolution task, where each example contains one text and two spans. The model is trained to determine whether the two spans refer to the same entity in the text. Since our model is pre-trained to predict meaningful spans, we conjecture that the model benefits from this training objective, so it is better at capturing the meaning of spans in the text.

We show an example as follows:

text: 这时候放在床上枕头旁边的手机响了，我感到奇怪，因为欠费已被停机两个月，现在它突然响了。(At this time, the mobile phone placed next to the pillow on the bed rang. I was surprised because it had been shut down for two months because of Arrears, and now it suddenly rang.)

Span1: 手机 (the mobile phone)

Span2: 它 (it)

Label: True

display_title: Limited technical contribution and weak baselines

content.title: Limited technical contribution and weak baselines
content.review:
The paper proposes to perform n-gram masking and predicting rather than token-level masking. n-grams with lengths up to N are first extracted and point-wise mutual information is used to filter out meaningless n-grams. Then pre-training with masking on these more meaningful n-gram/phrases are performed.

1) The idea of performing mask on filtered n-gram is quite incremental and the technical contribution is very limited.
2) Baseline is weak: there have been many pretrained language models (e.g., RoBERTa, XLNet, spanBERT) proposed in the past year which show improved performance over BERT. However, the author only uses BERT as baseline and failed to compare with more recent BERT-variants.

To sum up, given the limited novelty and weak experiments, this paper is below the bar of acceptance for ICLR.

content.title: Response to Reviewer2
content.comment:
Thanks for the valuable feedbacks.

1.Baseline is weak.

We have updated our baseline models:

1)We trained BERT with the same number of additional steps as BURT.

2)We trained a SpanBERT model by replacing our masking module with a random span masking strategy while keeping the other hyperparameters unchanged. 

3)We use the released sentence embedding toolkit LASER (https://github.com/facebookresearch/LASER) as a baseline of retrieval tasks.

Results on CLUE and analysis are reported in Table 2. CMNLI is no longer available on the official evaluation server and it is replaced with OCNLI since October 22. Therefore, we report results on OCNLI instead. We observe that BERT with additional MLM steps can hardly bring any improvement except for the WSC task. SpanBERT is effective on WSC but is comparable to BERT on other tasks. Overall, both BURT and BURT-wwm-ext outperform the baseline models on 4 out of 6 tasks. Especially, BURT obtains improvements of 3.45% over the updated BERT and 2.07% over SpanBERT on WSC. 

Results on FAQ and NLG are reported in Table 4~5. We provide more examples of paragraphs retrieved by different models in Table 6. Our BURT yields the highest accuracy (82.2%) and MRR (0.872) among all the evaluated models on FAQ. LASER is comparable to SpanBERT and BURT on FAQ but is less effective on NLG, probably because the sentence embedding model is not suitable for tasks where different granular linguistic units are involved at the same time.

display_title: Incremental paper; less than satisfactory experiments

content.title: Incremental paper; less than satisfactory experiments
content.review:
This paper introduces the idea of universal representation learning and presents a pre-trained language model that maps different granular linguistic units into the same vector space. The model is a simple and intuitive extension to BERT. Experiments are performed on a Chinese retrieval and language generation task.

Strengths:
The ides of mapping different linguistic units into the same vector space is interesting and potentially impactful.
The application of the pre-trained model to the retrieval and generation task where linguistic units of different granularity are retrieved or generated (instead of paragraph retrieval or token level generation) is interesting and also potentially useful.

Cons:
The paper is clearly an engineering effort with some simple modifications to BERT pre-training. I do not see how this is scientifically very interesting. The comparison with BERT on Chinese retrieval and language generation task is not appropriate. Instead we should consider Chinese BERT or multilingual BERT as comparison. We could also consider comparing this to SpanBERT.
More clear comparison with token level masked pre-training strategies on established benchmarks would help make the contribution more apparent. As the moment, it is hard to judge the impact of the pre-trained model.

content.title: Experiments could have been more comprehensive
content.review:
This paper presents a method to develop contextual language models which capture different granularities of linguistic information. The approach is similar to BERT, but instead of masking only tokens, the authors select ngrams based on high PMI score. The masking objective is then to predict the full ngram given the context. The method is evaluated on the CLUE dataset, and shows improvements across a wide range of tasks requiring different granularities of information. The paper also introduces two new datasets to evaluate retrieval performance using their contextual language model.

I am not convinced with certain parts of the evaluation. The objective mentioned is very similar to SpanBERT, and I was interested in an explicit comparison with SpanBERT. Probably the "span" row in Table 7 is showing that, but it was not clear. Even then, I would be interested to see if the trend holds in English. Its important to know if the advantages are due to Chinese segmentation challenges or are more general. 

The retrieval tasks do not have a strong baseline. A very relevant baseline will be LASER (https://github.com/facebookresearch/LASER), which can be directly applied to Chinese text. 

Minor comments:
1.  Certain statements are not well supported with evidence, better to remove : "which is not applicable when multiple levels of linguistic units are involved at the same time", " to encode different levels of linguistic unit into the same vector space", "achieving encouraging performance at a certain level of linguistic unit but less satisfactory results at other levels."

2. Why remove the longest n-gram ? You can create different masking examples out of the overlapping ngrams.

3. It was tricky for me to review since I dont know much about CLUE. I will advise introducing relevant tasks of CLUE with an example.

4. Same with BERT-wwm-ext. It is not common knowledge, so better to introduce it briefly with citation.

content.title: Response to Reviewer5
content.comment:
Thanks for the valuable feedbacks.

1.Need an explicit comparison with SpanBERT.

We have made additional experiments.

1)We trained BERT with the same number of additional steps as BURT as our new baseline.

2)To compare BURT with SpanBERT, we trained a SpanBERT model by replacing our masking module with a random span masking strategy while keeping the other hyperparameters unchanged.

3)The corresponding results and analysis are reported in Table 2 and Section 4.1. (CMNLI is no longer available on the official evaluation server and it is replaced with OCNLI since October 22. Therefore, we report results on OCNLI instead.) 

We observe that BERT with additional MLM steps can hardly bring any improvement except for the WSC task. SpanBERT is effective on WSC but is comparable to BERT on other tasks. Overall, both BURT and BURT-wwm-ext outperform the baseline models on 4 out of 6 tasks. Especially, BURT obtains improvements of 3.45% over the updated BERT and 2.07% over SpanBERT on WSC. 

2.Is the n-gram masking method general?

Our method is general and is not limited to any specific language.

Due to the large size of the English corpus and limited computational resources, we may not be able to complete the required experiments during the rebuttal phrase but we will complete these experiments in our future work.

However, our previous work indirectly explains that using PMI to extract meaningful segments from the English corpus is also effective. Specifically, we train a Transformer-based model with a vocabulary containing n-grams with high PMI scores. The model is evaluated on an English analogy dataset, where our method brings about 25% absolute accuracy improvement. Unfortunately, we are unable to provide the corresponding article due to the double-blind policy.

3.The retrieval tasks do not have a strong baseline.

We apply LASER to both FAQ and NLG tasks and the results are updated. On FAQ, our BURT yields the highest accuracy (82.2%) and MRR (0.872) among all the evaluated models. LASER is comparable to SpanBERT and BURT on FAQ but is less effective on NLG, probably because the sentence embedding model is not suitable for tasks where different granular linguistic units are involved at the same time. We also show more examples in Table 6. Please refer to Table 4-6 and Section 4.2-4.3 for more details. 

4.Introduce relevant tasks of CLUE with an example.

We provide examples for each classification task of CLUE as follows.

AFQMC: Given two sentences, the model need to determine whether they have similar meanings. 

Sentence1: 商家怎么开通花呗支付 (How do merchants activate Huabei payment) 

Sentence2: 为什么无法开通花呗 （Why can't I activate Huabei?）

Label: 0

TNEWS’: Short sentence classification. 

sentence: 通过中介公司买了二手房，首付都付了，现在卖家不想卖了。怎么处理？ （I bought a second-hand house through an intermediary company and paid the down payment. Now the seller does not want to sell it. How to deal with it?） 

label: 106 

label_des: news_house

IFLYTEK: Long sentence classification. 

sentence: 朴朴快送超市创立于2016年，专注于打造移动端30分钟即时配送一站式购物平台。…成为一家让社会尊敬的互联网公司。(Pupu Express Supermarket was founded in 2016, focusing on creating a one-stop shopping platform for instant delivery in 30 minutes on the mobile terminal…. It has become an Internet company respected by the society.) 

label: 110 

label_des: 社区超市 (Community supermarket)

OCNLI: Natural language inference task, a combination of XNLI and MNLI. 

sentence1: 一点来钟时,张永红却来了。(It was about one o'clock, but Zhang Yonghong came.) 

sentence2: 一点多钟,张永红来了。（After one o'clock, Zhang Yonghong came.）

 gold_label: entailment

WSC: Coreference resolution task.

text: 这时候放在床上枕头旁边的手机响了，我感到奇怪，因为欠费已被停机两个月，现在它突然响了。(At this time, the mobile phone placed next to the pillow on the bed rang. I was surprised because it had been shut down for two months because of Arrears, and now it suddenly rang.) 

Span1: 手机 (the mobile phone) 

Span2: 它 (it)

Label: True

CSL: Each example contains a text and several keywords. The model needs to determine whether these keywords are true labels of the text. 

Text: 介绍了国内外以冶金矿渣、尾矿渣及粉煤灰、城市垃圾焚烧飞灰为主要原料的废渣微晶玻璃的研究概况.…最后展望了工业及生活废渣制备微晶玻璃的未来发展. (This article introduces on glass-ceramics using metallurgical slag, tailings slag, fly ash, and Fly ash from municipal waste incineration….Finally, it briefly introduce the future development of glass-ceramics prepared from waste slags.) 

keyword: [矿渣, 彩色微晶玻璃, 粉煤灰] 

label: 1

5.Introduce BERT-wwm-ext briefly with citation. 

We have made an update in Related Work: “the latest BERT-wwm-ext … perform MLM on a higher linguistic level, the masked segments (whole words…)” and in the second paragraph of Section 3.3.2 Traning Details: “We use the pre-trained BERT and BERT-wwm-ext for initialization, … the latter is trained from the Chinese BERT using whole word masking on extended data (Cui et al., 2019).”
